fixes.explanation: Nice-sounding guess, but James doesn't promise money or honor here. He says perseverance finishes its work so that you may be “…mature and complete, not lacking anything.” That's about who his brothers become, not what they collect. Later in this very passage, he even says the rich man will fade away.

Strong sounds good, but feared isn't what James says here. He says perseverance finishes its work so that you may be “…mature and complete, not lacking anything.” Nobody's being scary in this verse. It's all about being complete.
God is the one to ask. James says, “Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God…” He points the one who lacks wisdom straight to God. And he adds right away that God gives generously.

That's a picture people may know, but it isn't the one James uses here. For the person who doubts, he says, “…he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind.” His picture is a wave, not a sheep.
Good image, but it isn't the one James uses here. He says the one who doubts “…is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind.” So the answer is the wave.

False, and James is plain about it. He says, “That man should not expect to receive anything from the Lord.” The man he means is the one who asks while doubting. In the verse before, James says that doubter is like a wave of the sea.
Secure would sound comfy, but James doesn't say it. He says the rich one should exult in his low position. Then he follows it by saying the rich man will pass away.
James says no to that. He writes that no one should say “God is tempting me.” Then he gives the reason: “For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone.” So it isn't fine to say it.
False, friend. James says no one should say “God is tempting me.” His reason is that “…God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone.” Nobody gets to pass the blame upstairs.

His own evil desires. James says, “But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed.” Each one means each one, so nobody gets a pass. It's his own desires doing the luring.

It gives birth to death. James says, “Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.” He lays out the chain step by step: desire, sin, then death. It's a heavy verse.
That would be nice, but James says something else. He says that sin, “…when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.” It's a heavy verse.
